content: Mithridate, also referred to as mithridatum, mithridatium, or mithridaticum, is a historical antidote believed to have been created by Mithridates VI of Pontus. This remedy, which reportedly contained up to 65 ingredients, was designed to counteract poisoning. It gained significant prominence during the Renaissance, particularly in Italy and France, where it was highly valued and remained in use for centuries. A later adaptation of this formula, known as theriac (Theriacum Andromachi), continued to be recognized well into the 19th century. The name mithridate originates from its creator, Mithridates VI, the King of Pontus. According to historical accounts, Mithridates fortified his body against poisons by regularly consuming antidotes and preservatives. This practice allegedly rendered him immune to toxins, to the extent that when he attempted suicide, he could not find a poison potent enough to kill him. The recipe for mithridate was discovered in his personal cabinet, written in his own handwriting, and was subsequently brought to Rome by Pompey. The formula was later translated into verse by the physician Servilius Damocrates and subsequently by Galen. Over time, the original recipe likely underwent significant modifications. Simon Kellwaye, in 1593, recommended a preparation involving a large onion hollowed out and filled with mithridate or theriac, along with rue leaves. Remarkably, physicians in London were still authorized to prescribe mithridate as late as 1786. Over time, the term mithridate came to signify any general-purpose antidote. Aulus Cornelius Celsus, in his work De Medicina (circa 30 AD), provided a detailed description of one version of the mithridate antidote. His translation lists the following ingredients: costmary (1.66 grams), sweet flag (20 grams), hypericum, gum, sagapenum, acacia juice, Illyrian iris (likely Iris germanica), cardamom (8 grams each), anise (12 grams), Gallic nard (Valeriana italica), gentian root, dried rose leaves (16 grams each), poppy tears (Papaver rhoeas), parsley (17 grams each), casia, saxifrage, darnel, long pepper (20.66 grams each), storax (21 grams), castoreum, frankincense, hypocistis juice (Cytinus hypocistis), myrrh, opopanax (24 grams each), malabathrum leaves (24 grams), flower of round rush, turpentine resin, galbanum, Cretan carrot seeds (24.66 grams each), nard, opobalsam (25 grams each), shepherd's purse (25 grams), rhubarb root (28 grams), saffron, ginger, and cinnamon (29 grams each). These ingredients were ground into a powder and mixed with honey. For poisoning, a dose the size of an almond was dissolved in wine, while for other ailments, a dose the size of an Egyptian bean was deemed sufficient. Certain ingredients in Celsus' formulation, such as Illyrian iris, darnel, and rhubarb, were not commonly found in other versions of the antidote. Celsus' account, written approximately 100 years after Mithridates' death, represents one of the earliest published versions of the formula. Galen referred to the antidote as theriac and documented various versions by Aelius (used by Julius Caesar), Andromachus (Nero's physician), Antipater, Nicostratus, and Damocratis. The formulation by Andromachus closely resembled that of Celsus. The production of antidotes labeled as mithridate or theriac (known in English as treacle) persisted into the 19th century. Ephraim Chambers, in his 1728 Cyclopaedia, described mithridate as a prominent medicine in apothecaries' shops, composed of numerous ingredients such as opium, myrrh, agaric, saffron, ginger, cinnamon, spikenard, frankincense, castor, pepper, and gentian. It was considered a cordial, opiate, sudorific, and alexipharmic. Petrus Andreas Matthiolus regarded mithridate as more effective against poisons than Venice treacle and noted that it was easier to prepare. Later versions of the antidote incorporated unconventional ingredients such as dried blood, dried lizard flesh, or viper flesh, as well as malabathrum. Despite its historical significance, mithridate faced criticism. Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History (circa AD 77), expressed skepticism about mithridate and other theriacs, particularly due to their extensive and complex ingredient lists. The legend of Mithridates and his antidote has also permeated literature. In A.E. Housman's poetry collection A Shropshire Lad, one poem highlights the remarkable abilities of King Mithridates and his antidote.
